content: Nafcillin is typically administered by a healthcare provider in a hospital or clinical setting. If you are storing nafcillin at home, do not share it with others, even if they have the same condition as you, as it may harm them. Always keep nafcillin out of the reach of children. Before using nafcillin, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any medications you are taking, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter (OTC) medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and other supplements. This information will help your provider determine if nafcillin is appropriate for you. Nafcillin may interact with other medications and supplements. Be sure to discuss with your healthcare provider if you are using any of the following: Tetracyclines (e.g., tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, omadacycline, sarecycline) Warfarin (a blood thinner) Cyclosporine (an immune system suppressant) Probenecid (commonly used for gout) This is not an exhaustive list of potential drug interactions, so always disclose all medications and supplements you are taking. If you are allergic to penicillin, other medications, corn, or corn products, inform your healthcare provider. Additionally, disclose if you have asthma, liver disease, kidney disease, a history of antibiotic-associated diarrhea, or if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It is not known if nafcillin can harm an unborn baby, so your provider will advise you on its use during pregnancy. If you are breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed, inform your provider, as nafcillin passes into breast milk. There are no known interactions between nafcillin and foods or drinks. However, the effects of alcohol on nafcillin are unknown. Heavy alcohol consumption can weaken your immune response, making it harder for your body to fight infections. If you accidentally use too much nafcillin, seek medical help immediately by calling 911 or contacting a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. Overdose may require discontinuation of the medication and supportive treatment by a healthcare provider. If you miss a dose of nafcillin, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take double or extra doses. It is crucial to complete the full prescribed course of nafcillin, even if your symptoms improve, to reduce the risk of antibiotic resistance. Nafcillin is an antibiotic used to treat infections caused by certain bacteria. It is not effective against viral infections (e.g., the common cold, influenza, or coronavirus) or non-bacterial infections. Using antibiotics unnecessarily can lead to resistance, making them less effective in the future. Nafcillin may also be used for other conditions as determined by your healthcare provider. Nafcillin works by killing bacteria through the inhibition of cell wall synthesis, which is essential for bacterial survival. Nafcillin is available in injectable forms, including: 1 g injection 2 g injection 10 g injection 20 mg/mL injection 2 g/100 mL injection It is usually administered as a liquid injected into a muscle or blood vessel by a healthcare provider. Common side effects of nafcillin include pain, swelling, or inflammation at the injection site and rash. If these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here, so contact your provider if you suspect any adverse reactions. Serious side effects of nafcillin, though less common, include severe allergic reactions, seizures, kidney damage, liver damage, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, and blood disorders. Symptoms of severe allergic reactions include difficulty breathing, wheezing, rapid heartbeat, fever, swollen lymph nodes, facial swelling, throat tightness, hives, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, stomach cramps, and joint pain. If you experience any of these, stop using nafcillin and seek emergency medical attention. Seizures have been reported in some individuals using nafcillin. Signs of a seizure include muscle twitching, jerking, spasms, tremors, stiffening of the arms and legs, confusion, dizziness, or loss of consciousness. If you experience these symptoms, stop using nafcillin and contact your healthcare provider immediately. Nafcillin can cause kidney damage. Symptoms include reduced urination, swelling in the feet or legs, weakness, difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, or nausea. If you notice these symptoms, contact your provider right away. Liver damage (hepatotoxicity) is another potential side effect. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, weakness, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stools, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Notify your provider immediately if you experience these symptoms. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), can occur during or up to two months after stopping nafcillin. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe stomach cramps, and fever. Contact your provider if you experience these symptoms. Nafcillin may also cause blood disorders, such as agranulocytosis, neutropenia, or bone marrow depression. Symptoms include fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual weakness, dizziness, or abnormal heartbeat. If you experience these, stop using nafcillin and seek medical attention. People allergic to nafcillin or any of its ingredients should not use this medication. Consult your pharmacist for a complete list of ingredients in the specific nafcillin product you are prescribed.
